questions.question: Which presentation is most concerning for possible pulmonary embolism requiring emergency evaluation?
choices: Hypotension with severe dyspnea and hypoxemia
A stable chronic cough
A routine medication question
A resolved minor ankle sprain
questions.explanation: Hypotension, severe respiratory distress, and hypoxemia may indicate high-risk PE and require emergency-level assessment.

questions.question: Why is unilateral leg swelling not diagnostic of DVT by itself?
choices: Cellulitis, injury, venous disease, lymphedema, and other conditions can mimic DVT
Leg swelling never occurs in DVT
Only PE causes swelling
Imaging is never useful
questions.explanation: DVT symptoms are nonspecific; clinical probability and appropriate diagnostic pathways are needed.

questions.question: What should be included when assessing suspected VTE probability?
choices: Symptoms, risk factors, alternatives, and validated diagnostic pathway
Only the patient’s age
Only the color of the leg
Only a medication refill history
questions.explanation: Safe VTE assessment integrates symptoms, risk factors, competing diagnoses, and validated diagnostic testing pathways.

questions.question: Which history can represent a major transient VTE provoking factor?
choices: Recent surgery, trauma, or hospitalization with immobility
Stable daily activity without risk factors
Correct use of compression instructions
A normal foot examination
questions.explanation: Surgery, trauma, and immobilization are important transient VTE risk factors that inform recurrence and duration discussions.

questions.question: Why should thrombophilia testing not be ordered reflexively during acute VTE care?
choices: It can be misleading and may cause harm if it leads to inappropriate labeling or treatment duration
It identifies every cause immediately
It replaces the VTE evaluation
It removes the need for anticoagulation safety review
questions.explanation: Testing should be ordered only when results would meaningfully change management, often with specialist guidance.

questions.question: Which item is essential at an anticoagulation follow-up visit?
choices: Confirm drug, dose, indication, adherence, organ function when relevant, interactions, bleeding, and access
Only measure temperature
Only repeat a remote imaging report
Ignore OTC NSAIDs and supplements
questions.explanation: Anticoagulation safety requires active reconciliation, monitoring, bleeding review, and practical access assessment.

questions.question: Which finding should prompt urgent assessment for possible anticoagulant-associated major bleeding?
choices: Melena, hematemesis, new neurologic symptoms, or head trauma
Stable appetite
A routine dental cleaning planned months away
Improved exercise tolerance
questions.explanation: GI bleeding, neurologic symptoms, or head trauma while anticoagulated can be serious and require urgent evaluation.

questions.question: What makes outpatient DVT/PE care potentially appropriate for a selected patient?
choices: Clinical stability, an appropriate plan, medication access, understanding, and reliable follow-up
Any diagnosis of PE regardless of stability
No ability to return for care
Uncontrolled bleeding
questions.explanation: Outpatient management is reserved for selected stable patients with safe treatment and reliable follow-up conditions.

questions.question: What should be reassessed after the primary treatment period for VTE?
choices: Recurrence risk, bleeding risk, provoking context, duration plan, and patient preferences
Only the diagnosis date
Only the patient’s shoe size
Nothing if symptoms improved
questions.explanation: Duration is individualized and should be reassessed rather than automatically stopped or continued without review.

questions.question: What is the FNP-level VTE principle?
choices: Treat anticoagulation as a one-time prescription
Integrate emergency triage, VTE context, medication safety, access, duration, and follow-up
Assume every swollen leg is DVT
Delay PE evaluation until symptoms worsen
questions.explanation: High-quality VTE care combines prompt recognition of danger with individualized, safe longitudinal anticoagulation care.
